newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Di Pietro says ex-PM Craxi out to ruin him.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Di Pietro says ex-PM Craxi out to ruin him.

text.p: Antonio Di Pietro, a hero in Italy for his judicial assault on corruption, on Monday accused his most famous target -- former prime minister Bettino Craxi -- of orchestrating a campaign to ruin him.

Di Pietro, 46, had been the star of an elite group of Milan magistrates, known as the "Clean Hands" pool, which brought down Italy's political establishment in a series of graft probes beginning in 1992.

"With the start of the 'Clean Hands' investigation and in parallel as it evolved, a violent campaign of defamation...was unleashed in order to block the investigations from going forward," Di Pietro said in a statement.
"The campaign was knowingly advanced by Craxi and others, all of whom I had regularly denounced to the courts," he said.
Craxi, the former Socialist Party leader, lives in self-imposed exile in Tunisia and says he is too sick with diabetes to return to Italy, where he has several convictions for graft.

Di Pietro unexpectedly quit as a magistrate two years ago, for reasons never fully explained, and last month resigned as public works minister when he himself came under investigation for alleged irregularities in his work as a magistrate.
On Monday, he found himself for the first time on the witness stand, called to testify at the trial of two of his former graft defendants accused of plotting to discredit him.
Businessman Paolo Berlusconi, brother of ex-prime minister Silvio, and former defence minister Cesare Previti deny the charges.
Di Pietro, after being mobbed by television cameras as he entered the courthouse in this northern town, exercised his right not to respond to questions.
He asked the judges if he could read a statement explaining his reasons for not testifying. When the judges refused his request, his lawyer gave out the text to journalists.
Premier from 1983 to 1987, Craxi faces a five and a half year prison sentence for illegal party financing which has been upheld on appeal.
He has appeals pending against three other court convictions for which he has been sentenced to jail terms totalling a further 20 years and three months.
Craxi, who often faxes statements to Italian news agencies, did not immediately comment on Di Pietro's remarks.

Di Pietro said in his statement that his lawyer had found documents to prove his accusations against Craxi, but said they and other papers relating to the Berlusconi-Previti trial had been seized in police raids of his offices and those of his attorneys earlier this month.

"In this situation it is impossible for me to reconstruct and prove that which I have been saying for a long time," Di Pietro said. "I have no choice but to exercise my right not to respond as a final form of civil and silent protest."
A verdict in the trial was expected on January 27.
